In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the mechanistic basis for the In(L50) vs In(H) adjustment equation for divalent transition metals and with understanding the mechanistics of the In(L50)-In(H) relationship for other toxicants.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a combination of the following three factors is the mechanistic basis for the observed relationship between LC50 and hardness: (1) the competitive binding of hardness and transition-metal cations to transition-metal binding sites on gills; (2) the competitive binding by carbonate and hardness cations to transition metal-binding sites on gills and; (3) aqueous complex formation of transition metals by carbonate and bicarbonate.

the slope of the ln(LC50)-ln(hardness) regression for a metal is ∼1 at midrange hardness if alkalinity covariates with hardness, but is ∼0.50 at midrange hardness when alkalinity is held at a constant value.
the In(LC) vs In(H) adjustment equation for transition metals is valid for a range of conditions, but the slope of the adjustment equation is not always ∼1.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the In(LC 50 ) versus ln(hardness ) adjustment equation for metals can be explained by a combination of (1) competitive binding of the metals, the hardness cations, as well as the protons, to the transition-metal-binding sites in the gills of fish, and (2) the aqueous complexation by HCO 3 and CO 2 2.
the slope of the ln(LC50)-ln(hardness) regression line is determined by the ratio of alkalinity to hardness in the water.

we have shown that the adjustment equation is mechanistically sound, that it works well for most metals and fish, that the equation is robust to changes in the hardness scale, and that the equation is useful for estimating the hardness sensitivity of metals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the slope of the ln(LC50)-vs-ln(hardness) regression is not an indicator of whether the metal toxicity is controlled by the metal or the metal ion.
the In(LC 50 ) vs In (hardness) adjustment equation can be used to estimate LC 50 values for fish exposed to metals in waters of unknown hardness.
the adjustment of metal toxicity by hardness is not due to the effect of hardness on the bioavailability of the metal.
